analysis.one_liner: Makes bankrupt oil, gas, and coal companies pay cleanup costs before shareholders and executives.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in May 2026 and has received no committee vote, hearing, or floor action, with 17 Democratic cosponsors and none from the other party.
analysis.plain_summary: When an oil, gas, or coal company goes bankrupt, cleanup of its wells, mines, and sites can be treated as an ordinary debt that gets wiped out, leaving taxpayers and nearby communities to pay. This bill changes the bankruptcy code so full reclamation costs are paid from company assets first, cannot be erased in bankruptcy, and can be recovered from parent companies, private equity firms, and hedge funds that own shares, plus clawed back from executives' pay if the estate falls short.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and communities near wells, mines, and refineries who currently can be stuck with cleanup bills when fossil fuel companies shed their obligations in bankruptcy. Workers at bankrupt fossil fuel companies also gain, since their unpaid wages and benefits would rank ahead of cleanup costs, which in turn rank ahead of shareholders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near fossil fuel sites

how_it_helps.text: Cleanup and reclamation costs would be treated as necessary expenses recovered from the property securing lenders' claims, rather than left behind in bankruptcy [S2].
Reclamation costs would rank ahead of unsecured claims and shareholders in the payment line, with environmental bond obligations and federal and state environmental penalties prioritized [S2].
Cleanup obligations could not be discharged in bankruptcy and fossil fuel assets could not be abandoned as burdensome by the estate [S2].

If the estate cannot cover worker wages and cleanup costs, the court could claw back executives' pay from the prior five years, and parent companies, private equity firms, and hedge funds owning shares would be strictly liable to cover the shortfall [S2].

A longer 10-year look-back would let trustees undo transfers made to insiders before bankruptcy [S2], and new federal oil, gas, and coal leases could not be transferred by a company that has filed for bankruptcy [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel company shareholders, secured lenders and bondholders, executives, and the private equity and hedge funds that invest in them would bear cleanup costs that bankruptcy currently lets them shed. Some of those higher financing and compliance costs could ultimately show up in energy prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel investors, executives, and lenders

drawbacks.text: Strict joint and several liability for parent companies, private equity firms, and hedge funds, plus five-year clawbacks of executive pay, would make fossil fuel investment riskier and more expensive, which could raise financing costs and potentially energy prices [S2].

The rules apply only to fossil fuel companies, so a good-faith objection is that other polluting industries in bankruptcy would still be able to shed cleanup obligations, and singling out one sector could push investment toward less-regulated foreign producers.

Making cleanup costs senior to most other claims and barring abandonment of fossil fuel assets could make it harder to restructure a failing company in ways that preserve jobs and going-concern value, since creditors would face larger losses earlier [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is shifting cleanup costs off taxpayers and onto the investors and executives who profited from the operations, which is a substantial public good in states with abandoned wells and mines. The main cost is higher risk and financing expense for the fossil fuel sector, and a real risk that some marginal companies fold rather than restructure, with job losses in the short run. On balance the bill's costs fall on concentrated investors while its benefits are public, but its strict-liability design is aggressive and untested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees in late May 2026, and neither committee has taken it up since, leaving it sitting with about seven months left in the Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Dave Min introduced the Ending Fossil Fuel Bailouts Act of 2026 on May 26, 2026 [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Natural Resources Committee, so both would need to act on it [S4].
The bill has 17 cosponsors, all House Democrats [S3].
No committee markup, hearing, or floor vote appears in the action history after the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel companies and their financiers are better off so far, because cleanup costs remain dischargeable in bankruptcy and taxpayers still absorb abandoned-site cleanup while the bill sits unactioned in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel companies and their investors

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, with no Republican support in the record.

industries.note: Cleanup and reclamation costs would survive bankruptcy, rank ahead of shareholders, and their assets could not be abandoned. This closes a path by which companies shed environmental obligations and the public pays for abandoned wells and mines.

industries.industry: Private equity firms and hedge funds invested in fossil fuels
industries.note: They would be strictly liable for a bankrupt company's unpaid cleanup costs, and a 10-year look-back would expose transfers to insiders. This raises the risk and cost of fossil fuel buyouts that currently can leave cleanup debts behind.
Reclamation costs would be recovered from the collateral securing their loans and ranked above their unsecured claims, reducing what they recover in a fossil fuel bankruptcy.
Up to five years of executive compensation could be clawed back when a bankrupt company cannot cover worker wages and cleanup costs.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action since referral, divided jurisdiction between two committees, no Republican cosponsors, and roughly seven months left in the session, the bill is very unlikely to receive a committee vote or floor action and will most likely die in committee when the Congress ends.
